← Electrical panel upgrade bid calculator

How much to charge to upgrade an electrical panel

The number a homeowner wants is a price per amp, or a published “$2,500 panel upgrade.” That number is not a takeoff. A 100A same-amp garage swap with the existing grounding is not the same job as a 100A-to-200A underground service with twenty AFCI breakers and a finished-space feeder. The starting amp is the same. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the feeder and the landing, not just the amp rating

EV-charger calculators price a dedicated circuit, a trench, and panel space. Standby-generator calculators price a transfer switch, a pad, and gas. Mini-split calculators price a line-set and one more circuit. A panel upgrade is a service: the can, the landing of every existing circuit, the path from the meter, grounding, and the utility. Quoting all of that from a published per-amp number is how the first underground lateral eats the field margin.

A job with the same starting amp can cost much more

Each finished-space feeder is fishing and patch that never appears on the label. An underground lateral is billed as its own hours and its own cable. AFCI/GFCI, a meter socket, new ground rods, and temporary power are adders that get forgotten on a brochure special. On the sample rates a 100A-to-200A underground job with a 40-foot finished-space feeder, twenty AFCI breakers, temp power, and a utility disconnect prices about $11,590 ($58 per amp of new service, 46.0 crew-hours). The same shop’s 100A same-amp garage swap prices about $2,941 ($29 per amp, 10.7 hours, walk-away $2,059). Matching the brochure job’s per-amp number on the underground upgrade is how that job becomes a loss.

A 400A class is not automatically the expensive one

A 200A-to-400A underground meter-main in a garage is not the 200A finished-space job plus 100%. On the sample rates that 400A class prices about $11,054 ($28 per amp, 39.8 crew-hours) — similar money to the 200A underground, not because the can is cheaper but because the 40-foot finished feeder and the twenty AFCI breakers do not live in a published per-amp number. A 100A-to-200A overhead garage meter-main with eight AFCI and new ground rods prices about $7,658 (28.0 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first utility disconnect.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $52/h journeyman loaded at 34% payroll burden is $69.68. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not an electrical specification, a building-code determination, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Ampacity, service path, grounding, meter, and whether the utility must disconnect are yours to confirm.

Price your panel upgrade

Common questions

How much to charge to upgrade an electrical panel?

Charge from the panel swap, any amp upgrade, overhead versus underground path, feeder feet, circuits landed, AFCI/GFCI, meter socket, new grounding, temporary power, utility disconnect, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 100A same-amp garage swap at the sample rates in this calculator prices around $2,941 — about $29 per amp of new service.

Why is a per-amp panel-upgrade quote dangerous?

Homeowners count the number on the label. Feeder feet, AFCI/GFCI, underground laterals, finished-space access, a meter socket, new grounding, and temporary power do not scale with that number. Matching a cheaper per-amp quote written for a brochure garage swap is how a 200A underground job becomes a two-day loss.

Does a higher amp rating always cost more to install?

Not in proportion. On the sample rates a 100A to 200A underground job with a 40-foot finished-space feeder, twenty AFCI breakers, temp power, and a utility disconnect prices around $11,590 ($58 per amp), while a 100A same-amp garage swap prices around $2,941 ($29 per amp).

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not electrical, construction, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

FOR LICENSED ELECTRICIANS

Bid the feeder, the circuits, and the utility.

Price a panel replacement or 100A-to-200A service upgrade the way the trade actually loses money: the can, the landing of existing circuits, AFCI/GFCI, feeder feet, overhead versus underground, new grounding, a meter socket, temporary power, and the utility disconnect. You get the bid, the price per amp of new service, and the walk-away number below which the job loses money.

The service

Start from a common job, then replace every figure with your takeoff. Changing panel style or path never overwrites a rate you already typed.

Your crew rates

A $52/h journeyman loaded at 34% is $69.68. Quoting the raw wage on a published per-amp special is how a finished-space 200A underground job that looked fine turns into a two-day loss after the first feeder pull.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

Where the hours go

    Where the cost goes

      Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Starting hours and material rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, an electrical specification, or a building-code determination — replace them with your own takeoff.

      Common questions

      Why is a “panel swap” quote so much cheaper than a “service upgrade”?

      Because they are two different jobs and only one of them touches the utility. A same-amp swap — 100A in, 100A out, the first preset here — is the panel, the breakers, and landing the circuits. The moment the new amperage is higher than the existing service, this calculator adds a service change on top: 6 more hours by default, plus whatever the mast or lateral, meter socket, grounding, temporary power, and utility coordination actually take. That is why a brochure price written for a swap is not a number you can hand a 100A-to-200A customer.

      What does going overhead vs. underground actually change?

      The cable rate and the dig. An overhead mast run starts at $8 a foot of SE cable plus a $185 mast and weatherhead kit, and no underground hours. An underground lateral drops the mast kit to zero but the cable starts at $14 a foot and the path adds 5 hours on its own. Feeder length is billed at 0.15 hours a foot either way, so a long lateral compounds: more hours per foot, pricier cable, and the trench time on top.

      Why does the panel location change the price when the panel is the same?

      Access. A garage or basement panel is worked on an open wall. A panel in finished living space adds 3 hours by default for protecting the room, cutting and patching, and working around what is in it — before any of the electrical work differs at all. It is the single easiest thing to miss when quoting from a photo, and the most common reason a finished-space job runs long.

      Why do circuits and AFCI breakers get counted one at a time?

      Because they are the part that scales with the house, not with the panel. Each circuit landed is 0.35 hours plus a $12 breaker; each AFCI or GFCI is 0.2 hours plus a $48 breaker. A ten-circuit garage panel and a thirty-circuit whole-house panel are the same box on a shelf and very different days of work — and a code cycle that requires AFCI on more circuits moves the breaker cost far more than it moves the labor.

      Does this include the permit and the utility fee?

      Both are their own inputs, starting at a $185 permit fee and a utility disconnect/reconnect fee you type yourself, because they are set by your jurisdiction and your utility and no calculator can know them. They are pass-through costs that still carry your overhead and margin here, so they land in the price rather than quietly coming out of it. Check both against your actual authority having jurisdiction before you send the bid.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. A share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your amperages, wages, or prices.

      What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

      The bid price already carries your target margin on top of labor, gear, fees, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — crew hours, the panel and breakers, SE cable, mast or lateral, meter socket, temporary power, permit and utility fees, travel and equipment — the point below which the job stops being profitable at all. Typing a number into “Price you’re considering” shows you the margin, or the loss, before you send it.

vs-a-flat-panel-upgrade-price.html.text:
← Electrical Panel Upgrade Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat panel-upgrade price

“A panel upgrade runs about $2,500” is not a price for a panel upgrade — it is a price for one feeder length, one circuit count, one path, and one answer about the utility, quietly quoted on every job that calls in.

What a flat panel-upgrade price is

A flat price is the fastest way to answer the phone: one number for “a panel upgrade”, sometimes dressed up as a dollars-per-amp rate so it looks like it flexes with the job. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between contractors, and it is the number a customer holding a neighbour’s invoice or a competitor’s quote will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set on one job — one amp rating, one overhead mast, a short feeder in an unfinished garage, the existing grounding left alone, no meter socket, no temporary power, no utility coordination — and then reused on every panel afterward, whether or not the next one looks anything like it.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the existing and new amp rating, whether the service is overhead or underground, whether the panel is a main-breaker can or a meter-main combo, whether it sits in a garage, a basement, or finished living space, how many feeder feet the run takes, how many circuits have to be landed and how many of those need AFCI or GFCI breakers, and whether the job includes a new meter socket, new grounding electrodes, temporary power, or utility coordination. Against your own loaded wage, overhead, travel, permit and utility fees, and target margin, it returns the bid price, the price per amp of new service, the effective hourly rate, and the break-even price below which the job loses money — for this panel, not a generic one.

What a flat panel-upgrade price doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same whether the feeder is eight feet across an open garage or forty feet through finished walls and ceilings. Prices feeder feet at their own hours-per-foot and cable cost, and adds finished-space access hours as a separate line.
Treats “landing the circuits” as one lump, whether there are ten of them or twenty with AFCI on every one. Prices circuits and AFCI/GFCI breakers separately, at both their own labour hours and their own material cost per breaker.
Prices an overhead mast swap and an underground service lateral as the same job. Carries a different cable cost per foot, a different mast kit, and separate underground path hours for each service type.
Has no line for a new meter socket, new ground rods, temporary power, or the hours spent coordinating with the utility. Each is its own toggle with its own hours and material, because each is present on some panel jobs and absent on others.
Gives the electrician a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the break-even price and the effective hourly rate, so a shopped or matched price can be scored against real cost before anyone commits to it.

Three jobs, the same flat number

Using this calculator’s own presets and its default crew rates, against a flat $2,500 panel-upgrade quote:

JobBreak-evenCalculator’s bidAgainst a flat $2,500
100A same-amp garage swap, overhead, existing grounding kept, 10 circuits (the brochure special) $2,058.60 $2,940.86 The flat price clears cost by $441.40, and gives up $440.86 of the margin this job could carry.
100A → 200A overhead garage, meter-main, new ground rods, 16 circuits, 8 AFCI $5,360.79 $7,658.27 The flat price is $2,860.79 below break-even — the job loses money before profit.
100A → 200A underground, 40 ft feeder through finished space, 20 AFCI, temp power, utility disconnect $8,112.83 $11,589.76 The flat price is $5,612.83 below break-even — the job loses more than twice the quote itself.

All three are “a panel upgrade”. The same flat number is generous on the first, loses money on the second, and is not close on the third. Run your own job in the calculator to see which side of that gap it falls on.

Why a per-amp rate does not fix it

The usual repair is to quote dollars per amp instead, so the number at least appears to scale with the service. On this calculator’s own defaults it scales the wrong way. The 100A same-amp garage swap prices at $29.41 per amp of new service. The 200A → 400A class change with a new meter-main prices at $27.63 per amp — less per amp, on a far larger job, because the fixed work (getting there, the permit, coordinating the utility, landing what is already there) does not double when the amp rating does.

So a per-amp rate derived from a small job overcharges every large one, and a rate derived from a large job undercharges every small one. Carry that per-amp rate onto the 200A underground job above and it quotes $5,881.71 — $2,231.12 under that job’s break-even. The rate is not merely imprecise; it points away from the cost.

A flat rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one job it was built for, and nothing about a flat number or a per-amp rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat panel-upgrade price get the bid wrong?

Because almost none of the labour scales with the words “panel upgrade”. The hours come from feeder feet, how many circuits have to be landed, how many of those need AFCI or GFCI breakers, whether the path is overhead or underground, whether the panel sits in a garage or in finished living space, and whether the utility has to be coordinated with at all. A flat price was set on one job with one answer to each of those questions, and then quoted on jobs with different answers.

Is a dollars-per-amp rate any better than a flat price?

No, and it can be worse, because it looks like it is adjusting for job size when it is not. Run this calculator’s own presets on its default rates: the 100A same-amp garage swap prices at $29.41 per amp of new service, while the 200A to 400A class change with a new meter-main prices at $27.63 per amp. The larger service is cheaper per amp, so a per-amp rate derived from a small job overcharges the large one and a rate derived from a large job undercharges the small one. The rate moves in the opposite direction from the cost.

What does a flat price leave out entirely?

The line items that turn a one-day job into a two-day one: the feeder run and its cable, the per-circuit landing time, AFCI and GFCI breakers at both their hours and their material cost, a new meter socket, new grounding electrodes, temporary power, utility coordination hours, and the permit and utility fees themselves. Each is its own input here, because each is present on some panel jobs and absent on others.

How far under water can a flat price actually put a job?

On this calculator’s defaults, a flat $2,500 panel-upgrade quote against its 100A to 200A underground preset - a forty-foot feeder through finished space, twenty AFCI circuits, temporary power and a utility disconnect - lands $5,612.83 below that job’s break-even price of $8,112.83. That is before any profit: the job loses more than twice the flat quote itself.

Is a flat panel-upgrade price ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs it can land close - same amp rating, same path, same panel location, a similar circuit count and a similar answer on grounding and the utility. A shop that only does same-amp garage swaps in one neighbourhood may quote a flat price for years without being bitten. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because nothing about a flat number tells you when the next job has stopped matching the one the number was built on.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It holds no data on local rates, competitors, or what a homeowner in your area expects to pay. It takes the wage, burden, overhead, travel, and target margin you enter and turns them into a break-even price and a bid price for the feeder, circuits, path, grounding, and utility work you describe. It replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not your judgment about your own market.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat panel-upgrade price is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the one the number was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it. It names no company or product: the comparison is against a pricing method, not against a competitor.

Open the Electrical Panel Upgrade Bid Calculator and price your own job, or read how much to charge to upgrade an electrical panel for the walkthrough.

This is a pricing worksheet built from your own assumptions. It is not a load calculation, not a code compliance check, and not a substitute for a licensed electrician’s judgment or the authority having jurisdiction.

← Electrical Panel Upgrade Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. ServiceTitan

Two different shapes: ServiceTitan is an account-based field service management platform for running an electrical company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one panel replacement or service upgrade cost, given its feeder, circuit landing, and path, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

ServiceTitan is a field service management platform, founded in 2007 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan, headquartered in Glendale, California. It serves HVAC, plumbing, electrical, and other trades with scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, marketing, reporting, and job costing across a whole business, with a mobile app for crews in the field. It is an account-based platform: you sign up and use it as an ongoing service across a whole company, not a one-off calculator. ServiceTitan's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — field service management software serving the electrical trade among others, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for ServiceTitan appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what ServiceTitan does. It does not schedule technicians, dispatch crews, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one job's service path (overhead mast or underground lateral), panel style, and panel location, with feeder feet, circuits to land, AFCI/GFCI breakers, meter socket replacement, new grounding, and temporary power as their own line items, plus loaded crew wage, payroll burden, permit fee, utility disconnect/reconnect fee, travel and equipment, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the bid price, the price per amp of new service, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Should I use this calculator or ServiceTitan?

They do different jobs, and an electrical shop of any size will likely end up touching both eventually.
